text: What motive? Money! M. Renauld was a millionaire several times over, and at his death (or so she and Jack believed) half that vast fortune would pass to his son. Let us reconstruct the scene from the standpoint of Marthe Daubreuil.
context: Poirot identifies money as Marthe's motive and begins her reconstruction.

text: Ah, but we did not leave her behind. She was out of the Villa Marguerite by the back way whilst we were talking to her mother in the hall. That is where, as the Americans say, she 'put it over' on Hercule Poirot!
context: Poirot admits Marthe escaped the Villa Marguerite before they left.

text: Now, to support this theory, the criminal must have been fully cognizant of Mr. Renauld's plans. That leads us to Madame Renauld. But facts fail to support any theory of her guilt. Is there any one else who might have known of them? Yes.
context: Poirot reasons that the killer had to know Renauld's plan and eliminates Madame Renauld.

text: No wonder the servants heard M. Renauld mounting the stairs; not a board of them but creaks fit to wake the dead!
context: Poirot observes that the creaking stairs should have exposed the alleged abduction.

text: Always the facts must be twisted to fit the theory! Did not Giraud find the traces of two persons, a man and a woman, in the shed? And how does that fit in with his reconstruction of the case? I will tell you—it does not fit in, and so we shall hear no more of them! I ask you, is that a methodical way of working?
context: Poirot attacks Giraud for twisting facts to fit his theory.

text: That will do very well. We shall just have time.
context: Poirot calculates that they have just enough time.

text: In that right-hand bed yonder. M. Bex says that they are the footmarks of the gardener. Let us see if that is so. See, he approaches with his wheelbarrow.
context: Poirot identifies which flower-bed he intends to test.

text: I am pleased with you. Go now and rest yourself. Hastings here and I have work to do. You shall see him tomorrow.
context: Poirot praises Dulcie and sends her to rest.

text: Has an English lady, Miss Robinson, arrived?
context: Poirot asks whether the disguised Dulcie has arrived.

text: I will ask you to go to the railway station and take a train to the next station along the line, Abbalac. Ask there at the cloak-room whether two foreigners deposited a valise there on the night of the murder. It is a small station, and they are almost certain to remember. Will you do this?
context: Poirot sends Jack on a fabricated railway inquiry.

text: You recognize it, my friend?
context: Poirot asks Hastings to recognize the photograph.

text: The murderer of M. Renauld, Hastings. And the would-be murderer of Madame Renauld.
context: Poirot identifies the dead woman as Renauld's murderer and Madame Renauld's attacker.

text: I beg your pardon, my friend—one can always be mistaken. Regard a great actress, does not her acting of grief carry you away and impress you with its reality? No, however strong my own impression and belief, I needed other evidence before I allowed myself to be satisfied. The great criminal can be a great actor. I base my certainty in this case, not upon my own impression, but upon the undeniable fact that Mrs. Renauld actually fainted.
context: Poirot warns that apparent emotion can be acted and demands evidence.

text: You speak as usual, without reflection, Hastings. In some cases two identical weapons _would___ be highly improbable. But not here. This particular weapon was a war souvenir which was made to Jack Renauld's orders. It is really highly unlikely, when you come to think of it, that he should have had only one made.
context: Poirot explains why two duplicate war-souvenir daggers are plausible.

text: It is to me incredible that the servants heard nothing. The creaking of that staircase, with _three___ people descending it, would awaken the dead!
context: Poirot doubts that three people could descend the creaking stairs unheard.

text: Ah, that, unfortunately, I cannot for the moment remember—but I shall do so. I had hoped you might be able to assist me.
context: Poirot admits he cannot yet recall the earlier crime but expects to.

text: The great Giraud! The great Giraud is nothing but a toy balloon—swollen with its own importance. But I, Hercule Poirot, whom he despises, will be the little pin that pricks the big balloon—_comme ça!___
context: Poirot compares Giraud to a swollen balloon and himself to the pin.

text: At last you have seen the detective you admire—the human foxhound! Is it not so, my friend?
context: Poirot teases Hastings about admiring Giraud's physical methods.

text: Naturally. And yet, do you know, Hastings, I doubt if his heart was ever seriously engaged. So far we have looked upon Bella Duveen as a siren, and Marthe Daubreuil as the girl he really loved. But I think that if we reversed the terms we should come nearer to the truth. Marthe Daubreuil was very beautiful.
context: Poirot re-evaluates Jack's feelings for Bella and Marthe.

text: _Mon Dieu!___ But it is that you have the susceptible heart!
context: Poirot comments on Hastings's susceptible heart.

text: Ah, that is the question! There we have the whole mystery. As yet, I cannot explain it. There is only one idea that presents itself to me as having a possible connection.
context: Poirot identifies the false time as the central mystery.

text: Would I do such a thing? I assure you that I have heard nothing whatsoever. Did you not observe the shock your news was to me?
context: Poirot denies having prior knowledge and points to his genuine shock.

text: And yet—I was not satisfied, _mon ami___. _I was not satisfied.…___
context: Poirot says Bella's confession still failed to satisfy him.

text: No, I shall await their return in the _salon___. It is cool there on this hot morning.
context: Poirot chooses to wait calmly in the salon.

text: She must have changed her room!
context: Poirot realizes Madame Renauld changed rooms.

text: You see now his annoyance at the inopportune visit of the girl Bella. Every moment of delay is fatal to his plans. He gets rid of her as soon as he can, however. Then, to work! He leaves the front door slightly ajar to create the impression that the assassins left that way.
context: Poirot explains Bella's dangerous delay and the staged open door.

text: (3) Marthe Daubreuil was the daughter of the notorious Madame Beroldy who in my opinion was morally and virtually the murderess of her husband, although it may have been Georges Conneau's hand which struck the actual blow.
context: Poirot cites Marthe's parentage and Madame Beroldy's moral guilt.

text: Still more romantic! The first _rencontre___ in the train from Paris, the second here. Journeys end in lovers' meetings, is not that the saying?
context: Poirot romanticizes Hastings's repeated encounters with Cinderella.

text: Not at all, since his evidence confirmed my theory. But _I___ should have wasted my time if _I___ had gone. It is the same with so called 'experts.' Remember the handwriting testimony in the Cavendish Case. One counsel's questioning brings out testimony as to the resemblances, the defence brings evidence to show dissimilarity. All the language is very technical.
context: Poirot explains why Japp's fieldwork confirmed rather than replaced his theory.

text: And without doubt we are not original in the idea, Hastings. The excellent Giraud, he also has probably made his inquiries.
context: Poirot assumes Giraud has also checked the railway station.

text: My friend, I am about to surprise you—to please you! I have taken your reproaches to heart! We will examine some footprints!
context: Poirot announces that he will examine footprints to please Hastings.

text: _Eh bien!___ And your indiscretions! You recount them not?
context: Poirot playfully asks Hastings to recount his indiscretions.

text: We agree, _mon ami___—at least as to the cause. But what exact motive underlay this procedure of M. Renauld's?
context: Poirot asks for the motive behind Renauld's change of will.

text: That is enough. He was desperately anxious for the girl to go. Why? Not only because the interview was unpleasant. No, it was the time that was slipping by, and for some reason time was precious.
context: Poirot infers that Renauld's urgency concerned slipping time.

text: I do not agree with you. I have a little idea that these footprints are the most important things we have seen yet.
context: Poirot declares the apparently irrelevant footprints important.

text: You believe, then, in birth and breeding?
context: Poirot probes Hastings's belief in birth and breeding.

text: The victim is a man of middle-age. His body was found in the locked shed near the scene of the crime and had been dead at least forty-eight hours. And it is most probable that he was stabbed in a similar manner to M. Renauld, though not necessarily in the back.
context: Poirot deduces the second victim's age, location, time of death, and wound before hearing details.

text: If I have offended your susceptibilities in any way, I demand pardon of you. You will understand better soon. But, believe me, I have striven to concentrate all my energies on the case.
context: Poirot apologizes for offending Hastings while defending his focus on the case.

text: And he had been dead—how long?
context: Poirot asks how long Renauld had been dead.

text: She is a woman of great force of character, and passionately devoted to her husband. They take counsel together. Renauld sees only one way of escape—death. He must appear to die, in reality escaping to another country where he will start again under an assumed name, and where Madame Renauld, having played the widow's part for a while, can join him. It is essential that she should have control of the money, so he alters his will.
context: Poirot explains how the Renaulds planned an apparent death and escape.

text: No—_and there ought to have been.___ Listen, Hastings. The gardener, Auguste, as you heard him say, planted both those beds the preceding afternoon. In the one there are plentiful impressions of his big hobnailed boots—in the other, _none!___ You see? Some one had passed that way, some one who, to obliterate their footprints, smoothed over the surface of the bed with a rake.
context: Poirot explains how the absence of footprints proves the flower-bed was raked.

text: Yet he wrote him affectionate letters to Paris?
context: Poirot tests the anger theory against Renauld's affectionate letters.

text: You recognize it—eh, Hastings?
context: Poirot asks Hastings to recognize a paper fragment.

text: But why did you not say so at the time, mademoiselle?
context: Poirot asks why Marthe did not identify the tramp earlier.

text: We shall never know. Madame is a lady who can keep her secrets. And I doubt very much if the police will ever find her.
context: Poirot predicts Madame Daubreuil will keep her secrets and evade police.

text: Their names are unknown, but they are presumed to be Chilians from Santiago. And now, mademoiselle, you see what comes of being young and beautiful! I have betrayed professional secrets for you!
context: Poirot gives Marthe a misleading answer and playfully blames her beauty.

text: Jack Renauld was presumably acquainted with the planning out of the golf course. He knew that the body would be discovered almost at once, when they started to dig the bunker.
context: Poirot notes Jack knew the golf-course plan would expose the body.

text: Ah! _je m'en fiche!___ Her case was certainly not interesting.
context: Poirot dismisses the Countess's case.

text: You will do nothing of the sort. I forbid it.
context: Poirot firmly forbids Hastings from seeing him off.

text: And then you showed me that letter from Mademoiselle Dulcie, and I saw a chance of settling the matter once for all. The original dagger was stolen by Dulcie Duveen and thrown into the sea—since, as she thought, it belonged to her sister. But if, by any chance, it was _not___ her sister's, but the one given by Jack to Marthe Daubreuil—why then, Bella Duveen's dagger would be still intact! I said no word to you, Hastings (it was no time for romance) but I sought out Mademoiselle Dulcie, told her as much as I deemed needful, and set her to search amongst the effects of her sister. Imagine my elation, when she sought me out (according to my instructions) as Miss Robinson with the precious souvenir in her possession!
context: Poirot explains how Dulcie's letter and the surviving dagger could test Marthe's guilt.

text: How they meant to manage the body business originally, I do not know—possibly an art student's skeleton—and a fire or something of the kind, but long before their plans have matured an event occurs which plays into their hands. A rough tramp, violent and abusive, finds his way into the garden. There is a struggle, M. Renauld seeks to eject him, and suddenly the tramp, an epileptic, falls down in a fit. He is dead. M. Renauld calls his wife. Together they drag him into the shed—as we know, the event had occurred just outside—and they realize the marvellous opportunity that has been vouchsafed them.
context: Poirot explains how the tramp's sudden death created the needed opportunity.

text: By the window, whilst we were battering at the door. Where is—the other?
context: Poirot identifies the silk ladder as an escape route.

text: Then I may ask a little favour of you?
context: Poirot politely asks Jack for a small favor.

text: but women are very unexpected.
context: Poirot remarks that women are very unexpected.

text: _Mon ami___—I know human nature. Throw together a boy young Renauld and a beautiful girl like Mademoiselle Marthe, and the result is almost inevitable. Then, the quarrel! It was money or a woman and, remembering Léonie's description of the lad's anger, I decided on the latter. So I made my guess—and I was right.
context: Poirot explains how human nature led him to infer Jack's love affair.

text: Not a particle, _mon ami!___ And for once, perhaps, it is a pity.
context: Poirot approves the study's cleanliness while noting its investigative disadvantage.

text: My friend, my friend, where are your wits wandering? Remember the fragment of cheque, and the fact that the name Bella Duveen was faintly familiar to Stonor, and I think we may take it for granted that Bella Duveen is the full name of Jack's unknown correspondent, and that it was she who came to the Villa Geneviève that night. Whether she intended to see Jack, or whether she meant all along to appeal to his father we cannot be certain, but I think we may assume that this is what occurred. She produced her claim upon Jack, probably showed letters that he had written her, and the older man tried to buy her off by writing a cheque. This she indignantly tore up.
context: Poirot reconstructs Bella Duveen's visit using the cheque and Stonor's memory.

text: Undoubtedly there was a secret in M. Renauld's life—there can be no doubt of that. On the other hand, the word Santiago, to my mind, is a red herring, dragged continually across the track to put us off the scent. It is possible that it was used in the same way on M. Renauld, to keep him from directing his suspicions into a quarter nearer at hand. Oh, be assured, Hastings, the danger that threatened him was not in Santiago, it was near at hand, in France.
context: Poirot identifies Santiago as a red herring and locates the danger in France.

text: And the inmates of the house, monsieur?
context: Poirot asks who else was in the household.

text: In the meantime I had taken steps to force Mademoiselle Marthe into the open. By my orders, Mrs. Renauld repulsed her son, and declared her intention of making a will on the morrow which should cut him off from ever enjoying even a portion of his father's fortune. It was a desperate step, but a necessary one, and Madame Renauld was fully prepared to take the risk—though unfortunately she also never thought of mentioning her change of room. I suppose she took it for granted that I knew. All happened as I thought.
context: Poirot explains how he forced Marthe into action through Madame Renauld's staged rejection.

text: The man bears no resemblance to M. Renauld, but he is middle-aged, of a usual French type. That is sufficient.
context: Poirot explains why the tramp's general type was sufficient for the deception.

text: You are what the Scotch people call 'fey,' Hastings. It presages disaster.
context: Poirot interprets Hastings's optimism as a bad omen.

text: Then it is a singular mistake that I have made there—for it is shared by the station staff. They say you arrived by the 11:40 train.
context: Poirot cites station staff against Jack's denial.

text: That when you have two crimes precisely similar in design and execution, you find the same brain behind them both. I am looking for that brain, M. Giraud—and I shall find it. Here we have a true clue—a psychological clue. You may know all about cigarettes and match ends, M. Giraud, but I, Hercule Poirot, know the mind of man!
context: Poirot declares that identical crimes reveal the same mind and contrasts himself with Giraud.

text: Comprehend you not that I have forbidden such a loaf—a loaf haphazard and shapeless, that no baker should permit himself to bake!
context: Poirot complains about the shapeless loaf.

text: And you would swear to that in a court of law?
context: Poirot asks whether Hastings would swear to his alibi claim in court.

text: A little word with you, mademoiselle, if it is permitted?
context: Poirot politely requests a private word with Marthe.

text: Oh, no, Hastings, she did not! She said she did—yes—but that was to save the man she loved from the guillotine.
context: Poirot explains that Bella falsely confessed to save Jack.

text: _Bien!___ Madame Renauld loves Georges Conneau. Who, then, is Georges Conneau?
context: Poirot asks who Georges Conneau must be if Madame Renauld loved him.

text: _Mon Dieu!___ But what an idiom! What does it mean?
context: Poirot reacts to Hastings's English idiom.

text: But yes, it is better so. Before, there was at all events a clear theory as to how and by whose hands he met his death. Now that is all gone. We are in darkness. A hundred conflicting points confuse and worry us.
context: Poirot welcomes confusion after the collapse of a simple theory.

text: Madame Renauld's of course. That is where _la mauvaise chance___ came in. Her hair, dark originally, is almost completely silvered. It might just as easily have been a grey hair—and then, by no conceivable effort could Giraud have persuaded himself it came from the head of Jack Renauld! But it is all of a piece.
context: Poirot identifies the dark hair as Madame Renauld's and explains Giraud's error.

text: _Enfin!___ You have arrived. And all by yourself. It is superb! Continue your reasoning. You are right.
context: Poirot enthusiastically praises Hastings for remembering Georges Conneau.

text: We talk at cross-purposes, my friend. Remember, it is two crimes we are investigating—for which, as I pointed out to you, we have the necessary two bodies. There, there, _ne vous impatientez pas!___ I explain all. To begin with, we apply our psychology. We find three points at which M. Renauld displays a distinct change of view and action—three psychological points therefore.
context: Poirot separates the two crimes and begins a psychological analysis.

text: The last train left Merlinville at seventeen minutes past twelve.
context: Poirot supplies the last train's departure time.

text: Well, why not? You should know my methods by now. All I ask is that you should report to me fully every day, and follow implicitly any instructions I may wire you.
context: Poirot, recovering from influenza, sends Hastings to investigate Hunter's Lodge.

text: Strange, We all have the little grey cells. And so few of us know how to use them. Good morning, Signor Ascanio.
context: Poirot challenges the official solution and questions Signor Ascanio.

text: I have employed my grey cells to some advantage. Come, Signor Ascanio, you visited the dead man on the Tuesday morning—that is so, is it not?
context: Poirot challenges the official solution and questions Signor Ascanio.

text: The sight of so many jewels makes me wish I had turned my brains to crime, instead of to its detection. What a magnificent opportunity for some thief of distinction! Regard, Hastings, that stout woman by the pillar. She is, as you would say, plastered with gems.
context: Poirot and Hastings discuss the jewels at the Grand Metropolitan.

text: But no, Hastings. It is *your* wits that go astray. Miss Marsh proved the astuteness of her wits and the value of the higher education for women by at once putting the matter in *my* hands. Always employ the expert. She has amply proved her right to the money.
context: Poirot realizes the final trick in Andrew Marsh's hidden-will puzzle.

text: We are about to descend after the method of the dustbins, No one will observe us. The Sunday concert, the Sunday 'afternoon out,' and finally the Sunday nap after the Sunday dinner of England—*le rosbif*—all these will distract attention from the doings of Hercule Poirot. Come, my friend.
context: Poirot prepares to investigate Montagu Mansions.

text: *Tout doucement, mon ami*. Have I said that I think anything? All I say is—it is a curious story. And there is nothing to throw light upon it; except perhaps the lady's name, eh, Hastings?
context: Poirot analyzes the suspiciously cheap flat and questions Hastings about the Robinsons.

text: No, that was Roger Havering's job—but it was a mistake on their part. It put me on the right track. A man who has committed a murder with a revolver which he found on the spot would fling it away at once, he would not carry it up to London with him. No, the motive was clear, the criminals wished to focus the interest of the police on a spot far removed from Derbyshire they were anxious to get the police away as soon as possible from the vicinity of Hunter's Lodge.
context: Poirot explains how Roger and Zoe Havering committed the murder.

text: I am most serious. Figure to yourself, my friend, that the real rent of those flats is £350. I have just ascertained that from the landlord's agents. And yet this particular flat is being sublet at eighty pounds! Why?
context: Poirot analyzes the suspiciously cheap flat and questions Hastings about the Robinsons.

text: Imbecile that I have been! Triple imbecile! Not again will I vaunt my little grey cells!
context: Poirot realizes the final trick in Andrew Marsh's hidden-will puzzle.

text: We cannot be sure. He knew young Bleibner too, remember, and may have suspected something, or, again, the doctor may have thought that a further death motiveless and purposeless would strengthen the coils of superstition. Furthermore, I will tell you an interesting psychological fact, Hastings. A murderer has always a strong desire to repeat his successful crime, the performance of it grows upon him.
context: Poirot exposes Dr. Ames and explains the murders connected with the tomb.

text: Old man Halliday is no fool. He would tie up her money pretty tight.
context: Poirot predicts that Halliday protected his daughter's fortune.

text: Ah, the poor little lady! *Elle n'est pas bien tombée!*
context: Poirot reacts sympathetically to Flossie's unhappy marriage.

text: They function, my good Japp; assuredly they do!
context: Poirot answers Japp's teasing question about his little gray cells.

text: As we have *carte blanche*, I shall expend threepence in ringing up the Ritz—where you may have noticed our Count is staying. After that, as my feet are a little damp, and I have sneezed twice, I shall return to my rooms and make myself a *tisano* over the spirit lamp!
context: Poirot states his next investigative step and his concern for his health.

text: Hastings, my hat. And the brush. So! My galoshes if it still rains!
context: Poirot directs Hastings to prepare his clothes before leaving.

text: The papers give a few details, but I would like you to confirm them.
context: Poirot asks Jane Mason to verify Flossie's clothing.

text: Monsieur, I did not. But to track footmarks, and recognize cigarette-ash is not sufficient for a detective. He must also be a good psychologist! I knew that you disliked and mistrusted your son-in-law. He benefits by your daughter's death; the maid's description of the mysterious man bears a sufficient resemblance to him.
context: Poirot explains how psychology revealed that Halliday was withholding evidence.

text: When Japp returned from his expedition, he confirmed all my deductions. He also told me that a well-known crook was passing the jewels. I knew that whoever it was would be the exact opposite of the man Jane Mason described. When I heard that it was Red Narky, who always worked with Gracie Kidd—well, I knew just where to find her.
context: Poirot explains how Japp's findings identified Jane Mason as Gracie Kidd.

text: A great precaution, but perhaps a day late,
context: Poirot gently mocks Japp's decision to watch Carrington.

text: Then there is nothing more to be said. I must decline the case.
context: Poirot threatens to withdraw when Halliday insists he has told everything.

text: You will permit me to put a few questions? Your mistress, she was quite as usual before starting yesterday morning? Not excited or flurried?
context: Poirot begins interviewing Jane Mason about Flossie's behavior.

text: No, that was Roger Havering's job—but it was a mistake on their part. It put me on the right track. A man who has committed a murder with a revolver which he found on the spot would fling it away at once; he would not carry it up to London with him. No, the motive was clear; the criminals wished to focus the interest of the police on a spot far removed from Derbyshire; they were anxious to get the police away as soon as possible from the vicinity of Hunter's Lodge. Of course, the revolver found at Ealing was not the one with which Mr. Pace was shot.
context: Poirot explains why the revolver found in Ealing exposed the criminals' plan.

text: That is true. The few cases I have had to decline did not fill me with any regret.
context: Poirot says the cases declined during his illness were uninteresting.

text: And yet it is true. *Bien sûr*, my friend, it is true! But to bring that precious pair to justice, that is another matter. Well, Japp must do what he can—I have written him fully; but I very much fear, Hastings, that we shall be obliged to leave them to Fate—or *le bon Dieu*—whichever you prefer.
context: Poirot insists on the solution but doubts the murderers can be brought to justice.

text: I think not. There is something peculiarly elusive about that housekeeper—don't you think so? It struck me at once.
context: Poirot rejects Hastings's expectation that the housekeeper will be found.

text: If you please, mademoiselle.
context: Poirot invites Violet Marsh to begin explaining her unusual business.

text: Clearly he made a second will, and then had workmen from Plymouth in to make a suitable hiding-place. Instead of wasting time, taking up the floor and tapping the walls, we will go to Plymouth.
context: Poirot tells Hastings that tracing the workmen is the efficient route to the hiding-place.

text: Who destroyed this? And what was their object?
context: Poirot examines the motive behind the destruction of the concealed will.

text: That is a little hard on you, mademoiselle, seeing that you were Mr. Marsh's only blood relation.
context: Poirot comments on the apparent harshness of Andrew Marsh's will to Violet Marsh.

text: I could swear that here we have no longer the personality of Mr. Marsh. But who else has been in the house? Only Miss Marsh; and she, if I mistake not, is also a young lady of method and order.
context: Poirot contrasts the dirty labeled envelope with the orderly habits of Marsh and his niece.

text: The letter disappeared. Still, that, as you say, may not necessarily mean that the murderer took it. When you first found the body, Parker may have abstracted the letter unnoticed by you.
context: Poirot approves Sheppard's distinction between the blackmailer and the murderer. (continued)

text: That she said good-night to her uncle? But me—I do not always believe what a young lady tells me—no, not even when she is charming and beautiful.
context: Poirot says he does not automatically believe even a charming young woman.

text: The big air, it is all very well outside, where it belongs. Why admit it to the house? But let us not discuss such banalities. You have something for me, yes?
context: Poirot complains about the English preference for fresh air indoors.

text: She _seemed_ a nice girl—yes.
context: Poirot repeats Dr. Sheppard's description of Ursula with a different emphasis.

text: This morning fresh developments have arisen. It seems now that Mr. Ackroyd was murdered, not at a quarter to ten, but _before_. Between ten minutes to nine, when Dr. Sheppard left, and a quarter to ten.
context: Poirot falsely advances the time of the murder to provoke Miss Russell.

text: Hercule Poirot does not run the risk of disarranging his costume without being sure of attaining his object. To do so would be ridiculous and absurd. I am never ridiculous.
context: Poirot insists that he would not risk disarranging his clothes without achieving his purpose.

text: Mademoiselle, it is the business of Hercule Poirot to know things. I know that you went out earlier in the evening, that you left a message in the summer-house to say what time you would be there.
context: Poirot explains how he knew Miss Russell arranged a meeting in the summer-house.

text: Oh! I comprehend perfectly; you have referred to me as comic—as, perhaps, ridiculous now and then? It matters not at all. Hastings, he also was not always polite. Me, I have the mind above such trivialities.
context: Poirot says he is above being offended by an unflattering portrayal.

text: It is very good that—yes, it is very good. Listen, I do in verity believe that this husband of yours is innocent—but the affair marches badly. If I am to save him, I must know all there is to know—even if it should seem to make the case against him blacker than before.
context: Poirot says he believes Ralph innocent but needs every fact, however damaging.

text: So I give you then, a little lecture. The first thing is to get a clear history of what happened that evening—always bearing in mind that the person who speaks may be lying.
context: Poirot begins a lesson by requiring a clear history while allowing for lies.

text: Ah! no. My theory is that the murderer wore gloves or wrapped something round his hand. After the blow was struck, he picked up the victim's hand and closed it round the dagger handle.
context: Poirot explains how the murderer could have placed Ackroyd's fingerprints on the weapon.

text: _Mais oui, mais oui._ I heard. I am not deaf—nor stupid, thank the good God! But see you, you approach the matter from the wrong—the wrong—premises, is not that the word?
context: Poirot tells Raglan that his reasoning begins from the wrong premises.

text: One prefers to remain incognito. I am not anxious for notoriety. I have not even troubled to correct the local version of my name.
context: Poirot explains that he prefers to remain incognito.

text: Decidedly you have cells of a kind. But it leaves a good deal unaccounted for.
context: Poirot credits Dr. Sheppard's theory but notes that it leaves facts unexplained.

text: Yes, I mean that. _At nine-thirty Mr. Ackroyd was already dead._ It was the dictaphone speaking—not the man.
context: Poirot reveals that Ackroyd was already dead at nine-thirty.

text: But yes. You will remember that every one agreed—you yourself included—that it took five minutes to walk from the lodge to the house—less if you took the short cut to the terrace. But you left the house at ten minutes to nine—both by your own statement and that of Parker, and yet it was nine o'clock as you passed through the lodge gates. It was a chilly night—not an evening a man would be inclined to dawdle; why had you taken ten minutes to do a five-minutes' walk?
context: Poirot explains the five-minute discrepancy between Sheppard's departure and arrival at the gate.

text: So you will tell me the whole story, will you not? From the beginning.
context: Poirot asks Ursula to tell her story from the beginning.

text: Messieurs et Mesdames, this reunion of mine is at an end. Remember—_the truth goes to Inspector Raglan in the morning_.
context: Poirot ends the reunion by repeating his warning that the truth will reach Raglan.

text: I know now something I wanted to know. Let us leave it at that.
context: Poirot says the experiment revealed what he needed to know.

text: The first fact was the telephone call. If Ralph Paton were indeed the murderer, the telephone call became meaningless and absurd. Therefore, I said to myself, Ralph Paton is not the murderer.
context: Poirot concludes from the meaningless telephone call that Ralph Paton was not the murderer.

text: And he is not the same man he was—say, a year ago. His moral fiber is blunted. He is desperate. He is fighting a losing battle, and he is prepared to take any means that come to his hand, for exposure means ruin to him. And so—the dagger strikes!
context: Poirot explains how moral deterioration leads the desperate blackmailer to murder.

text: She had heard from some one that morning—some one addicted to drugs, she read the article in the paper, and she came to you to ask a few tentative questions. She mentioned cocaine, since the article in question was on cocaine. Then, when you seemed too interested, she switched hurriedly to the subject of detective stories and untraceable poisons. I suspected a son or a brother, or some other undesirable male relation.
context: Poirot explains how the goose quill, newspaper article, and medical questions revealed Miss Russell's connection. (continued)

text: Every one concerned in them has something to hide.
context: Poirot states that everyone concerned has something to hide.

text: If he is a scoundrel, he is a scoundrel on a mean scale. He has not the big ideas. That leaves us as a possibility, Raymond, or—well—Major Blunt.
context: Poirot uses Parker's finances and temperament to reassess the suspects. (continued)

text: Have I not told you at least thirty-six times that it is useless to conceal things from Hercule Poirot?
context: Poirot reminds Sheppard that concealment from him is useless.

text: I must be more careful of his _amour propre_. And now that we are left to our own devices, what do you think, my good friend, of a little reunion of the family?
context: Poirot jokes about protecting Raglan's pride and proposes a family meeting.

text: The fire, my friend. Ackroyd himself may have destroyed that letter, blue envelope and all, after you left him.
context: Poirot proposes that Ackroyd himself may have destroyed the letter.

text: I had connected her with the unknown man long before we actually came face to face with him. As soon as we found that quill. The quill suggested dope, and I remembered your account of Miss Russell's visit to you. Then I found the article on cocaine in that morning's paper. It all seemed very clear.
context: Poirot explains how the goose quill, newspaper article, and medical questions revealed Miss Russell's connection.

text: And now we come to the second fact—the chair pulled out from the wall. Inspector Raglan dismissed that as of no importance. I, on the contrary, have always regarded it as of supreme importance.
context: Poirot identifies the displaced chair as the second fact of supreme importance.

text: Is that the exact truth you are telling me there, M. l'Inspecteur?
context: Poirot challenges whether Raglan truly took everyone's fingerprints.

text: There seems no doubt that the man who was talking to Mr. Ackroyd in the library at nine-thirty could not possibly have been your son. Be of good courage, mademoiselle. All will yet be well.
context: Poirot reassures Miss Russell that the evidence separates her son from the voice in the study.

text: If you doubt me, ask her yourself, monsieur. But perhaps you no longer care to—the affair of the money——
context: Poirot encourages Blunt to ask Flora directly about her feelings.

text: To find out about the fire, I must ask the man whose business it is to observe such things. You permit——
context: Poirot explains why the proper witness must be asked about the fire. (continued)

text: You comprehend me? But Captain Ralph Paton must be cleared—_ça va sans dire_. I should suggest that you finish that very interesting manuscript of yours—but abandoning your former reticence.
context: Poirot requires Ralph's exoneration and a truthful conclusion to Sheppard's manuscript.

text: I who speak to you—I know the murderer of Mr. Ackroyd is in this room now. It is to the murderer I speak. _To-morrow the truth goes to Inspector Raglan._ You understand?
context: Poirot tells the murderer in the room that the truth will go to Raglan the next day.

text: You have the intelligence so quick! No, he has not been found at Liverpool. Inspector Raglan was very loath to let me send this paragraph to the press, especially as I could not take him into my confidence. But I assured him most solemnly that very interesting results would follow its appearance in print, so he gave in, after stipulating that he was, on no account, to bear the responsibility.
context: Poirot admits that the newspaper report of Ralph's arrest is false and predicts results.

text: The housekeeper, Miss Russell, who came to consult you on that Friday morning—is it indiscreet to ask what passed at the interview—apart from the medical details, I mean?
context: Poirot carefully asks what Miss Russell discussed during her medical visit.

text: Mr. Ackroyd had promised to invest in a dictaphone, you remember. Me, I had the curiosity to inquire of the company in question. Their reply is that Mr. Ackroyd _did_ purchase a dictaphone from their representative. Why he concealed the matter from you, I do not know.
context: Poirot reveals that Ackroyd did purchase a dictaphone.

text: I will take you the way that I have traveled myself. Step by step you shall accompany me, and see for yourself that all the facts point indisputably to one person. Now, to begin with, there were two facts and one little discrepancy in time which especially attracted my attention.
context: Poirot invites Sheppard to retrace the solution step by step and begins with the telephone call.

text: It is that there are moments when a great longing for my friend Hastings comes over me. That is the friend of whom I spoke to you—the one who resides now in the Argentine. Always, when I have had a big case, he has been by my side. And he has helped me—yes, often he has helped me. For he had a knack, that one, of stumbling over the truth unawares—without noticing it himself, _bien entendu_.
context: Poirot explains why he misses Hastings during difficult cases.

text: But most of my successes have been obtained by the aid of the police. I admire enormously your English police. If Inspector Raglan permits me to assist him, I shall be both honored and flattered.
context: Poirot praises the English police while requesting permission to assist.

text: I think you are. I fancy you were born in Kent.
context: Poirot infers that Charles Kent may have been born in Kent.

text: Now that you remind me of the fact, it is true that there is one thing more. It would be most unwise on your part to attempt to silence me as you silenced M. Ackroyd. That kind of business does not succeed against Hercule Poirot, you understand.
context: Poirot warns Sheppard that an attempt to silence him would fail.

text: You know the result of her investigations. Ralph Paton _had_ had a pair of boots with him. The first question I asked him when he came to my house yesterday morning was what he was wearing on his feet on the fatal night. He replied at once that he had worn _boots_—he was still wearing them, in fact—having nothing else to put on.
context: Poirot confirms that Ralph wore boots on the night of the murder.

text: But the inmates of the house had shoes soled with crepe rubber, and I declined to believe in the coincidence of some one from outside having the same kind of shoes as Ralph Paton wore. Charles Kent, as we know from the barmaid of the Dog and Whistle, had on a pair of boots 'clean dropping off him.' (3) Those prints were made by some one deliberately trying to throw suspicion on Ralph Paton. To test this last conclusion, it was necessary to ascertain certain facts. One pair of Ralph's shoes had been obtained from the Three Boars by the police.
context: Poirot rejects coincidence and considers deliberate evidence against Ralph.

text: After certain necessary formalities, I was allowed to bring him away. He arrived at my house in the early hours of yesterday morning.
context: Poirot explains how he deduced that Sheppard hid Ralph in a nursing home. (continued)

text: Will you be seated? Dr. Sheppard is so kind as to permit me the use of his surgery for a little conversation I am anxious to have with you.
context: Poirot politely receives Miss Russell in the borrowed surgery.

text: Was he hard pressed for money?
context: Poirot quickly asks whether Ralph Paton was short of money.

text: _Mais oui._ Do you realize that there are three separate motives staring us in the face. Somebody certainly stole the blue envelope and its contents. That is one motive. Blackmail! Ralph Paton may have been the man who blackmailed Mrs. Ferrars.
context: Poirot lays out three separate motives apparently implicating Ralph Paton.

text: I admit nothing that is not—_proved_!
context: Poirot refuses to accept any fact that has not been proved.

text: No, me, I will promenade myself in the grounds. I will rejoin you by the lodge gates in a quarter of an hour's time.
context: Poirot says he will walk in the grounds while Sheppard delivers the invitation.

text: But we must not lose sight of one thing.
context: Poirot accepts Sheppard's psychological explanation but warns against overlooking motive.

text: I consult Mademoiselle Sheppard as to suitable homes. She gives me the names of two near Cranchester to which her brother has sent patients. I make inquiries. Yes, at one of them a patient was brought there by the doctor himself early on Saturday morning. That patient, though known by another name, I had no difficulty in identifying as Captain Paton.
context: Poirot explains how he deduced that Sheppard hid Ralph in a nursing home. (continued)

text: The study of human nature, monsieur!
context: Poirot identifies his former profession as the study of human nature.

text: Let us go over all the main facts quietly and methodically. Recount them to me, Hastings, in an orderly and lucid fashion.
context: Poirot asks Hastings to summarize the Yellow Jasmine case.

text: *Mais non*, not Madame Olivier. *Cela va sans dire!* There are not many geniuses of her stamp in the world. No, I referred to the other lady--the lady on the stairs.
context: Poirot corrects Hastings about which woman he found unusual.

text: But yes! You know my motto--Be prepared. As soon as I found that the Countess Rossakoff was mixed up with the Big Four, I had every possible inquiry made as to her antecedents. I learnt that she had had a child who was reported to have been killed, and I also found that there were discrepancies in the story which led me to wonder whether it might not, after all, be alive.
context: Poirot explains how advance inquiries produced leverage with the countess.

text: But no! I appeal to your imagination, and you can suggest nothing more subtle than bombs in the fireplace. Well, well, I have need of some matches, I will promenade myself despite the weather. Pardon, my friend, but is it possible that you read *The Future of the Argentine*, *Mirror of Society*, *Cattle Breeding*, *The Clue of Crimson* and *Sport in the Rockies* at one and the same time?
context: Poirot dismisses Hastings's crude threat theory and notices the disordered books.

text: Madame, I--I who speak to you, swear once more. *I will bring the dead to life.*
context: Poirot promises the countess that he can restore her lost child.

text: You talk of evidence, but what evidence have we against him? True, we have a body, but we have no proof even that the man was murdered--prussic acid, when inhaled, leaves no trace. Again, we can find no one who saw any one enter the flat during our absence, and we have found out nothing about the movements of our late friend, Mayerling....
context: Poirot analyzes the lack of usable evidence against Number Four.

text: And if it is not work, it is the games, the sport. All those things they take _au grand sérieux. Now, madame, recount to me exactly, in detail, and as methodically as you can, the exact circumstances of your husband's disappearance.
context: Poirot reassures Mrs. Halliday and asks for a methodical account.

text: That is not exactly the point I had in mind, Hastings. If only one window was open it would not intrigue me so much. It is both windows being open that strikes me as curious.
context: Poirot focuses on the unusual state of the windows near Mayerling's body.

text: This gives one furiously to think, does it not?
context: Poirot reacts to Abe Ryland's angry letter.

text: What you think is always so important to yourself, Hastings. But let us pass from the mystery of the Yellow Jasmine to the Mystery of the Curry.
context: Poirot dismisses Hastings's judgment about the dying message.

text: Number Four succeeds for the opposite reason--he succeeds by the way of obscurity. Who is he? Nobody knows. What does he look like? Again nobody knows.
context: Poirot explains that Number Four's anonymity is his protection.

text: If you fire, you commit murder watched by ten pairs of eyes, and you will be hanged for it. This place is surrounded--has been for the last hour--by Scotland Yard men. It is checkmate, Mr. Abe Ryland.
context: Poirot reveals the police ambush at the quarry.

text: *Mon ami*, he overlooked the little gray cells of Hercule Poirot.
context: Poirot names Number Four's decisive mistake.

text: He has been gagged, Hastings. Gagged and then poisoned.
context: Poirot identifies signs of murder on Mayerling's body.

text: We know that he is a man of medium height, and of medium or fair colouring. If he were a tall man of swarthy complexion he could never have passed himself off as the fair stocky doctor. It is child's play, of course, to put on an additional inch or so for the part of James, or the Professor. In the same way he must have a short straight nose. Additions can be built on to a nose by skilful make up, but a large nose cannot be successfully reduced at a moment's notice.
context: Poirot infers Number Four's natural appearance from the limits of disguise.

text: Wilson was not poisoned, he was electrocuted. A thin metal rod passes up the middle of one of those chessmen. The table was prepared beforehand and set upon a certain spot on the floor. When the bishop was placed upon one of the silver squares, the current passed through Wilson's body, killing him instantly. The only mark was the electric burn upon his hand--his left hand, because he was left-handed.
context: Poirot explains the mechanism that killed Gilmour Wilson.

text: we leave that to Giraud and his friends. Hercule Poirot's methods are his own. Order and method, and 'the little gray cells.' Sitting at ease in our own arm-chairs we see the things that these others overlook, and we do not jump to the conclusion like the worthy Japp.
context: Poirot contrasts his methods with those of more conventional detectives.

text: See you, Hastings, we have to contend against four adversaries; that is, against four different personalities. With Number One we have never come into personal contact--we know him, as it were, only by the impress of his mind--and in passing, Hastings, I will tell you that I begin to understand that mind very well--a mind most subtle and Oriental--every scheme and plot that we have encountered have emanated from the brain of Li Chang Yen.
context: Poirot separates the Big Four into distinct personalities and methods.

text: But yes, that was a famous idea of yours--that and the books. See you, if they should say to me any time. 'That friend of yours, that Hastings, he has not the great brain, is it not so?' I shall reply to them: 'You are in error.' It was an idea magnificent and superb that occurred to you there.
context: Poirot praises the warning signs Hastings left in the flat.

text: if you wish you may wait in to put salt on the little bird's tail, but for me I do not waste my time so.
context: Poirot dismisses Hastings's hope that the false asylum attendant will return.

text: But yes, my friend, it is I. Brother Achille has gone home again--to the land of myths. It was I all the time. It is not only Number Four who can act a part.
context: Poirot reveals that Achille was his own disguise.

text: Your reasoning is at fault, Hastings. Employ the little gray cells. If your enemies wished to deceive you they would assuredly have seen to it that the Chinaman spoke in intelligible pigeon English. No, the message was genuine.
context: Poirot explains why the dying Chinaman's obscure message was genuine.

text: For you have a part to play, Hastings. An important part! Without you, I might well fail. Nevertheless, I felt that it was my duty to urge you to remain behind.
context: Poirot admits that Hastings is important to the final plan.

text: To startle him at a moment when he must act quickly or not at all. And we have this great advantage--he does not know that we recognise him. He thinks that he is safe in his new disguise. How I bless Flossie Monro for telling us of that little habit of his.
context: Poirot explains why he revealed himself to Number Four at dinner.

text: I am glad that Desjardeaux is convinced at last. *Eh bien*, then, we will start--or rather, I will start. You, Hastings, will remain here--yes, I pray of you. In verity, my friend, I am serious.
context: Poirot tries to leave Hastings behind before the final operation.

text: You do not see? No more did I. But I see now. Hastings, *I was being got out of the way*.
context: Poirot explains why he abandoned the train to Southampton.

text: We are going to think. Yes, here and now, we are going to exercise our little gray cells. This M. Halliday now, was he really in Paris? Yes, for Professor Bourgoneau, who knows him, saw and spoke to him.
context: Poirot stops to reason through Halliday's verified movements.

text: And to what end? Can we produce anything to impress a coroner's jury of your solid Britishers? Is our description of Number Four of any value? No; we shall allow them to call it 'Accidental Death,' and may be, although I have not much hope, our clever murderer will pat himself on the back that he deceived Hercule Poirot in the first round.
context: Poirot explains why he will not reveal his theory at the inquest.

text: 'Will you walk into my parlour, said the spider to the fly?' That is your little English nursery rhyme, is it not? No, no--they are subtle--but not so subtle as Hercule Poirot.
context: Poirot recognizes the dropped address as a deliberate trap.

text: He is a supreme artist in the way he sinks himself in each part he plays.
context: Poirot characterizes Number Four as an actor who disappears into roles.

text: It is necessary for this reason--Grant is not the murderer.
context: Poirot tells Inspector Meadows why he must interview Grant privately.

text: Belladona in the eyes, the sacrifice of the moustaches, and a real scar the inflicting of which caused me much pain two months ago--but I could not risk a fake beneath the eagle eyes of Number Four. And the final touch, your own knowledge and belief that there was such a person as Achille Poirot! It was invaluable, the assistance you rendered me, half the success of the coup is due to you!
context: Poirot explains the physical and psychological details of the Achille disguise.

text: Monsieur, if a doctor walks along the street and an accident happens, does he say, 'I have retired from my profession, I will continue my walk,' when there is some one bleeding to death at his feet? If I had been already in Nice, and the police had sent to me and asked me to assist them, I should have refused. But this affair, the good God thrust it upon me.
context: Poirot explains why he assists when a case is placed directly before him.

text: I said to myself, 'If you want to know anything about the dramatic profession there is one person who knows all that is to be known and that is my old friend, Mr. Joseph Aarons.'
context: Poirot flatters theatrical agent Joseph Aarons before seeking information.

text: I tell you I know what happened as well as though I had been there. You went into her compartment and you found her dead. I tell you I know it. To lie to me is dangerous. Be careful, Mademoiselle Mirelle.
context: Poirot warns Mirelle that lying to him is dangerous because he knows what happened.

text: It is my fancy, perhaps, but I think that you have a yearning in you for interesting happenings. *Eh bien*, Mademoiselle, all through my life I have observed one thing--'All one wants one gets!' Who knows?
context: Poirot reads Katherine's appetite for adventure and reflects on desire.

text: Yes, yes, I know. Life is like a train, Mademoiselle. It goes on. And it is a good thing that that is so.
context: Poirot compares life to a train that continues onward.

text: I am not mad. I am eccentric, perhaps--at least certain people say so; but as regards my profession, I am very much, as one says, 'all there.' I ask you, Monsieur Van Aldin, whether you would be glad or sorry if what I tell you should be the case?
context: Poirot distinguishes eccentricity from professional madness and asks Van Aldin to face his feelings.

text: Supposing, my good Georges, that you had been born in the same social sphere as your late master, Lord Edward Frampton--that, penniless yourself, you had married an extremely wealthy wife, but that that wife proposed to divorce you, with excellent reasons, what would you do about it?
context: Poirot asks George how an aristocrat might resist a justified divorce.

text: Leave it in the hands of Hercule Poirot, have no fears. I will discover the truth.
context: Poirot grandly assures Van Aldin that he will discover the truth.

text: You do not see why I am being so impertinent, Mademoiselle? I am an old man, and now and then--not very often--I come across some one whose welfare is dear to me. We are friends, Mademoiselle. You have said so yourself. And it is just this--I should like to see you happy.
context: Poirot explains that friendship makes Katherine's happiness important to him.

text: I was not aware that the fact had been mentioned outside the Examining Magistrate's office.
context: Poirot catches Mirelle referring to confidential knowledge.

text: But like all great men--and the Marquis was a great man--he had his weaknesses. He fell genuinely in love with Miss Grey, and suspecting her liking for Derek Kettering, he could not resist the temptation to saddle him with the crime when the opportunity presented itself.
context: Poirot identifies jealousy as the Marquis's decisive weakness.

text: So far the Comte could have been hidden to a marvel. No one knows of his presence on the train except Madame; he has been careful that the maid did not see his face. All that she could say is that he was tall and dark. It is all most conveniently vague.
context: Poirot highlights the convenient vagueness in the maid's description.

text: You will pardon an old man, Monsieur, if he says to you something that you may consider impertinent. There is one of your English proverbs that I would quote to you. It says that 'it is well to be off with the old love, before being on with the new.'
context: Poirot warns Derek with an English proverb about ending one romance before beginning another.

text: I have my own methods. The exercise of a little tact, a little cleverness--and the thing is done.
context: Poirot attributes his success in breaking an alibi to tact and cleverness.

text: *I am not concerned with the recovery of these jewels. That is the affair of the police.* I am working not for the police but for M. Van Aldin. I want to lay hands on the man who killed Madame Kettering. I am interested in the jewels only in so far as they may lead me to the man.
context: Poirot states that he seeks the murderer rather than the stolen jewels.

text: You are the daughter of your father, Mademoiselle Zia. To know when to stop. Ah! that is the art.
context: Poirot praises Zia for knowing when to stop gambling.

text: I am silent, but all the same I say it is a pity. And now, Messieurs, let us come to business.
context: Poirot ends a personal digression and turns the men back to business.

text: Dressed in that very sumptuous fur coat and the little red lacquer hat jammed down over her eyes, with just a bunch of auburn curls showing over each ear, it was no wonder that the conductor was deceived. He had not previously spoken to Mrs. Kettering, you remember.
context: Poirot details the disguise that deceived the conductor.

text: The psychology is at fault. The Comte is a scoundrel--yes. The Comte is a swindler--yes. The Comte preys upon women--yes. He proposes to steal Madame's jewels--again yes.
context: Poirot separates the Comte's known vices from the psychology of murder.

text: Do not enrage yourself, I beg of you. Every one has his own methods. Me, I have always found it a delightful and pleasing idea to combine business and pleasure together.
context: Poirot defends combining business with pleasure.

text: Mademoiselle, what you have said there is very just--very true. I was struggling in darkness, and you have shown me a light. There was a point that puzzled me and you have made it plain.
context: Poirot tells Lenox that her idea has illuminated a point that puzzled him.

text: It is not an uncommon thing to find when investigating a crime and it rouses an immediate question, the question of identity. That naturally was the first thing that occurred to me. Was the dead woman really Mrs. Kettering?
context: Poirot explains why a disfigured face raises the question of identity.

text: Yes, Mademoiselle. It was you who gave me the first inkling of the truth when you said that the person who committed the crime need not have been on the train at all. Before that, I could not see how the thing had been done.
context: Poirot credits Lenox with the insight that first opened the solution.

text: If you do not tell me the truth, I can do nothing.
context: Poirot refuses to proceed while Van Aldin withholds the truth.

text: What will you; it is my little hobby, to know things. Naturally I have the time to indulge it. I am not overburdened with affairs.
context: Poirot modestly calls gathering information his hobby.

text: I have been the cat, watching at the mouse hole. I have been the good dog following up the scent, and not taking my nose from the trail. And also, my good Georges, I have been the squirrel. I have stored away the little fact here, the little fact there. I go now to my store and I take out one particular nut, a nut that I stored away--let me see, seventeen years ago.
context: Poirot compares his method of storing facts to a squirrel collecting nuts.

text: That suggested camouflage. When I was in London I went to the surgeon in question, and I got several technical details from him which confirmed me in that belief. I mentioned the name of that surgeon in Knighton's hearing the day before yesterday. The natural thing would have been for Knighton to mention that he had been attended by him during the War, but he said nothing--and that little point, if nothing else, gave me the last final assurance that my theory of the crime was correct.
context: Poirot explains how Knighton's false limp became the final confirmation of his theory.

text: *Mon Dieu*, but that is something I have not thought of! We must break our journey in Paris. Quick, quick, let us alight at once.
context: Poirot suddenly insists on breaking the journey in Paris.

text: Yes, yes, it is as I say. You tell your lies and you think nobody knows. But there are two people who know. Yes--two people. One is *le bon Dieu*--
context: Poirot says both God and another observer know when people lie.

text: On the contrary, I think it agrees with them very well. Au revoir, Messieurs; if news of any importance comes to me I will communicate it to you immediately.
context: Poirot says new information about the Marquis fits his private ideas.

text: That is the simplicity of the whole thing. *There was no man.* Ah--*mille tonnerres!*--do you not see the cleverness of it all? Whose word have we for it that there ever was a man there? Only Ada Mason's. And we believe in Ada Mason because of Knighton's evidence that she was left behind in Paris.
context: Poirot reveals that the supposed man seen in Paris never existed.

text: *Then how did he know about them?*
context: Poirot asks how Derek knew about the rubies when no one had told him.

text: And trust Hercule Poirot. He knows.
context: Poirot closes by asking Lenox to trust both the train and him.

text: *Ah, ça par exemple*, that is of no importance whatever. Naturally, if he committed the crime he will have an alibi. A man with the Comte's experience does not neglect to take precautions. No, I said *if* for a very different reason.
context: Poirot dismisses the importance of an alibi for an experienced criminal.

text: I will ask you nothing. It is enough for me that it is as I thought. And I—I, too, have an instinct. We are working together towards a common end.
context: Poirot accepts Miss Howard's unspoken suspicion without forcing a confession.

text: Bah! Do not ask me to believe that any man could be so idiotic! Only a lunatic, who wished to commit suicide by causing himself to be hanged, would act so!
context: Poirot rejects the idea that Alfred openly bought poison and created obvious suspicion.

text: See you, one should not ask for outside proof—no, reason should be enough. But the flesh is weak, it is consolation to find that one is on the right track.
context: Poirot celebrates external confirmation of a deduction about the cut bell wire.

text: But I am most serious. Ah, there is something there that I do not understand. My instinct was right.
context: Poirot insists that Cynthia's coffee habit confirms an unresolved instinct.

text: The instinct that led me to insist on examining those coffee-cups. *Chut!* no more now!
context: Poirot explains his instinct and abruptly ends the discussion.

text: somebody stepped on that cup, grinding it to powder, and the reason they did so was either because it contained strychnine or—which is far more serious—because it did not contain strychnine!
context: Poirot explains the two possible motives for destroying the coffee cup.

text: But I must ask you to trust me. Now your help may be very valuable to me. I will tell you why. Because, in all this house of mourning, yours are the only eyes that have wept.
context: Poirot appeals to Miss Howard's genuine grief and asks for her trust.

text: Throughout the case, there have been evidences that the tragedy was intended to take place on Monday evening. On that day, Mrs. Inglethorp's bell wire was neatly cut, and on Monday evening Mademoiselle Cynthia was spending the night with friends, so that Mrs. Inglethorp would have been quite alone in the right wing, completely shut off from help of any kind, and would have died, in all probability, before medical aid could have been summoned. But in her hurry to be in time for the village entertainment Mrs. Inglethorp forgot to take her medicine, and the next day she lunched away from home, so that the last—and fatal—dose was actually taken twenty-four hours later than had been anticipated by the murderer; and it is owing to that delay that the final proof—the last link of the chain—is now in my hands.
context: Poirot reconstructs the murderers' original schedule and isolation plan.

text: You are not pleased with me, *mon ami?*
context: Poirot notices Hastings's irritation after rejecting his cocoa theory.

text: See; say that it is I who have committed this murder, I can think of seven most plausible stories! Far more convincing than Mr. Inglethorp's stony denials!
context: Poirot boasts that even a guilty man could invent a better defence than Alfred's.

text: The case is not clear yet—no. For it is of the most complicated! It puzzles *me*. *Me*, Hercule Poirot! There are two facts of significance.
context: Poirot admits the case challenges even him before identifying two major facts.

text: But I am most serious. Ah, there is something there that I do not understand. My instinct was right.
context: Poirot insists that Cynthia's coffee habit confirms an unresolved instinct.

text: I have no authority to go through these papers. But it should be done—at once!
context: Poirot refuses to inspect the victim's papers without authority while stressing their urgency.

text: it is not as though there was a blood tie. She has been kind and generous to these Cavendishes, but she was not their own mother. Blood tells—always remember that—blood tells.
context: Poirot interprets the family's restrained grief after Mrs. Inglethorp's death.

text: Probably not, but do you notice anything that strikes you as peculiar about this box?
context: Poirot asks Hastings to inspect the empty sleeping-powder box.

text: Was Dr. Bauerstein here on Tuesday evening? Here? And you never told me? Why did you not tell me? Why? Why?
context: Poirot erupts when Hastings reveals Bauerstein visited on the murder night.

text: It is evident! I had an idea—but clearly I was mistaken. Yes, altogether I was mistaken. Yet it is strange. But no matter!
context: Poirot reacts to testing the coffee cups and temporarily rejects an idea.

text: Shall I tell you why you have been so vehement against Mr. Inglethorp? It is because you have been trying to believe what you wish to believe. It is because you are trying to drown and stifle your instinct, which tells you another name——
context: Poirot interprets Miss Howard's vehemence as an effort to suppress another suspicion.

text: Who? That is the question. Why? Ah, if I only knew.
context: Poirot separates the unknown identity and motive behind the forced lock.

text: I do not mind telling you—though, as you know, it is not my habit to explain until the end is reached. The present contention is that Mrs. Inglethorp died of strychnine poisoning, presumably administered in her coffee.
context: Poirot reluctantly begins explaining his concern about the timing of the poison.

text: but it was not his candle that made this great patch, for you perceive that this is white grease; whereas Monsieur Lawrence's candle, which is still on the dressing-table, is pink. On the other hand, Mrs. Inglethorp had no candlestick in the room, only a reading-lamp.
context: Poirot uses the colour of the wax to exclude Lawrence's candle.

text: This time it is an idea gigantic! Stupendous! And you—*you*, my friend, have given it to me!
context: A remark by Hastings triggers Poirot's decisive realization.

text: But in the case of Alfred Inglethorp, all that is changed. His clothes, his beard, the glasses which hide his eyes—those are the salient points about his personal appearance.
context: Poirot explains why Alfred's conspicuous appearance is easy to imitate.

text: Still you are right in one thing. It is always wise to suspect everybody until you can prove logically, and to your own satisfaction, that they are innocent.
context: Poirot states his rule of universal provisional suspicion.

text: This attitude of his gave me furiously to think, and I was slowly forced to the conclusion that Alfred Inglethorp wanted to be arrested. *Eh bien!* from that moment, I was equally determined that he should not be arrested.
context: Poirot explains his strategic response to Alfred's plan.

text: In all this, you see, I think of that poor Mrs. Inglethorp who is dead. She was not extravagantly loved—no. But she was very good to us Belgians—I owe her a debt.
context: Poirot explains the personal obligation driving his investigation.

text: Does the next fit in with that? *A merveille!* Good! We can proceed.
context: Poirot tests whether the next fact fits the developing chain of reasoning.

text: And, then, there was that rather over-vehement hatred of hers! It concealed a very opposite emotion. There was, undoubtedly, a tie of passion between them long before he came to Styles.
context: Poirot interprets Miss Howard's hatred as concealment of passion for Alfred.

text: Bah! Do not ask me to believe that any man could be so idiotic! Only a lunatic, who wished to commit suicide by causing himself to be hanged, would act so!
context: Poirot rejects the idea that Alfred openly bought poison and created obvious suspicion.

text: It must have been done since yesterday, otherwise a good housemaid would have at once removed it with blotting-paper and a hot iron. One of my best hats once—but that is not to the point.
